CVE-2026-47261.title: Wasmtime is a runtime for WebAssembly. In versions prior to 24.0. ...
CVE-2026-47261.description: Wasmtime is a runtime for WebAssembly. In versions prior to 24.0.9, 36.0.10, and 44.0.2, when a filesystem preopen is given DirPerms::all() and FilePerms::READ without FilePerms::WRITE, this access control mechanism can be bypassed via the wasip2 descriptor.open-at or wasip1 path_open interfaces by opening a file with only the OpenFlags::TRUNCATE oflag. The root cause is that the clause handling OpenFlags::TRUNCATE in crates/wasi/src/filesystem.rs (Dir::open_at, lines 967–969) did not set open_mode |= OpenMode::WRITE;, which is later used for the access control check against FilePerms to determine whether opening the file is permitted; the single-line fix adds that missing assignment, after which the affected calls correctly fail with error-code.not-permitted and ERRNO_PERM respectively. Only wasmtime-wasi embeddings that combine DirPerms::MUTATE with FilePerms::READ are affected by this bug. In particular, the Wasmtime project's wasmtime-cli's use of wasmtime-wasi is not affected, because it always sets FilePerms::all() for all preopens. This issue has been fixed in versions 24.0.9, 36.0.10 and44.0.2.

CVE-2026-54786.description: Wasmtime is a runtime for WebAssembly. This bug only affects the native implementation of WASIp1, meaning that only runtimes which load core wasm modules and expose fd_renumber are affected. Runtimes are additionally only affected if they expose the ability to acquire a file descriptor, such as opening a file. For runtimes that deny access to files they are unaffected. This issue has been fixed in versions 24.0.10, 36.0.11, 44.0.3, and 45.0.2.

GHSA-5qpp-g3j2-8frx.title: Guests can send absolute-form HTTP requests to different hosts
GHSA-5qpp-g3j2-8frx.description: ### Summary Wasmtime's implementation of `wasi:http` in the `wasmtime-wasi-http` crate did not check that the value a guest passes to `set-path-with-query` on an outgoing request is actually a path. Absolute-form values such as `http://other.example/x` were accepted and written verbatim as the request target of the HTTP/1.1 request line, while the connection and the `Host` header used the authority the guest set with `set-authority`: ``` GET http://other.example/x HTTP/1.1 host: allowed.example ``` Wasmtime only connects to the authority the guest set, and any sort of request filtering based on host is done by the authority the guest set as well. However, RFC 9112 requires a server receiving an absolute-form target to ignore `Host`, so if the allowed authority is a forward proxy or a gateway that honors absolute-form targets, it forwards the request to `other.example`. A guest may then reach hosts the embedder did not have visibility into or allow. Both `wasi:http@0.2` and `wasi:http@0.3` are affected, including guests run with `wasmtime serve` and `wasmtime run -S http`. ### Impact This issue can cause hosts using the `wasmtime-wasi-http` crate to erroneously have requests sent to hosts that are otherwise explicitly disallowed in filtering policies. ### Patches Wasmtime 36.0.18, 48.0.6, and 49.0.3 have all been released which fixes this issue.

GHSA-6fr9-xmw9-5352.title: Unchecked memory usage in transferring borrowed resources between components
GHSA-6fr9-xmw9-5352.description: ### Summary Wasmtime contained a denial-of-service vulnerability where host memory could arbitrarily be consumed by transferring borrowed resources between components. This is similar to a previous vulnerability GHSA-q554-3cjc-rx7p but affects a different path which was not fixed there. Specifically when a component receives a borrowed resource that it defined itself there is no handle counter incremented charged to the store, but Wasmtime still allocated host memory to track this borrow. This memory allocation wasn't accounted for anywhere and guests could make this memory grow arbitrarily large. ### Details Wasmtime's tracking of `borrow<T>` handles in the component model employs host-allocated resources to be able to handle what happens when a function returns and undo the 'lends' of the `own<T>` resource they originally came from, as required by component model semantics. This tracking is handled specially, according to the component model, when a component receives a borrow for a resource it itself defines. In this situation the component does not receive a handle but instead receives its internal representation. This difference means that the mitigation implemented in GHSA-q554-3cjc-rx7p is bypassed as there's no handle that's charged to the store which is limited by default. Combined together it means that a lent borrow is untracked memory not limited by any means. ### Impact This is a denial-of-service vulnerability for Wasmtime where a guest can consume arbitrary host memory. Hosts are affected in default configurations and there is no known mitigation for this. Affected hosts are recommended to update to a patched version.

GHSA-h4wp-g4x3-7398.title: wasi-http p2: outgoing content-length can be invalid or not match body
GHSA-h4wp-g4x3-7398.description: ### Summary The wasmtime-wasi-http p2 implementation can, in some cases, send multiple conflicting content-length headers, or a content-length header which does not match the body length. This can expose other HTTP implementations to request smuggling attacks, bypassing the access control mechanisms built into wasmtime-wasi-http. ### Details This bug is related to GHSA-r8xh-cgf7-392j, which fixed wasmtime-wasi-http's handling of invalid content-length headers. The remediation of that bug unintentionally left one gap in enforcement. When a wasip2 guest receives a content-length header (or multiple, conflicting content-length headers) in an HTTP response, and then uses that headers resource to construct a HTTP request, and that request is sent without setting a body, the request will contain the response's content-length headers, and those could be conflicting and (unless it is the benign `content-length: 0`) will not match the body length. This particular pattern of use was, we believe, the only corner case not covered by previous remediation and testing. ### Impact This could enable HTTP request/response smuggling attacks (CWE-444) when used to send a request to a server which does not correctly implement HTTP. This attach mechanism could potentially bypass the access control mechanisms used by wasmtime-wasi-http embedders to restrict the destination of an HTTP request.

GHSA-m9f7-9w4p-gv38.title: Filesystem sandbox escape when renaming symlinks with trailing slashes
GHSA-m9f7-9w4p-gv38.description: ## Impact Wasmtime's filesystem implementation provided in the `wasmtime-wasi` crate contained a bug which allowed guests to escape their filesystem sandbox and read/write external directories. Guests provided write-access to any directory within their sandbox could move any directory on the filesystem the host process could access into their sandbox, and then read and write its contents. This bug is a full filesystem sandbox escape for guests. This bug is closely related to [GHSA-vqjp-4c8c-hfgg](https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/security/advisories/GHSA-vqjp-4c8c-hfgg). When renaming a file or directory, `wasmtime-wasi` strips a trailing slash from the source path to resolve its parent directory, but then re-appends the slash to the final path component before passing it to the `renameat` syscall. A guest could create a relative symlink pointing outside of its sandbox, for example `symlink('../outside', 'up')`, and then rename `'up/'` to a path within its sandbox. The host kernel would then follow the trailing-slash symlink and move the directory outside of the sandbox into the sandbox. The fix for GHSA-vqjp-4c8c-hfgg only changed how paths are opened, not how they are renamed, so this affects all published versions of Wasmtime at the time of this advisory's publication. This bug does not affect users on Linux or Windows, where `renameat` does not follow a symlink with a trailing slash. Users on macOS or FreeBSD, however, are affected by this issue. Only symlinks to directories can be used to escape the sandbox in this manner. ## Patches Wasmtime 36.0.18, 48.0.6, and 49.0.3 are being released with this advisory which patches this issue. ## Workarounds There is no known workaround for this issue. Users are recommended to upgrade to a patch release of Wasmtime that contains a fixed version of `wasmtime-wasi`. ## References * [GHSA-vqjp-4c8c-hfgg](https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/security/advisories/GHSA-vqjp-4c8c-hfgg) * bytecodealliance/wasmtime#14663 (the related `remove_dir` case)

GHSA-q554-3cjc-rx7p.title: Component-model handle tables are capped only per instance and charged to no limit
GHSA-q554-3cjc-rx7p.description: ### Summary A malicious guest can drive unbounded host memory growth using only component-model resource handles, with no linear memory, no core tables, no host imports, and default configuration. ### Impact Each guest `resource.new` allocates a slot in the owning component instance's host-side handle table. Allocation is bounded only by a per-table cap and is charged to no `ResourceLimiter` or `StoreLimits`, so `-W max-memory-size` and the embedder's configured memory and table limits do not bound it. Because the cap is per component instance, a single component can exceed it many times over by instantiating a sub-component repeatedly. ## Patches Wasmtime 49.0.3, 48.0.6, and 36.0.18 have been fixed by introducing a store-wide limit on the number of simultaneously-live component-model handles. - Default limit: **100,000 live handles per store** (~2.4 MB of handle-table memory). - New embedder knob: `Store::set_max_component_handles(n)` to raise or lower it. - New CLI flag: `-S max-component-handles=N` for `wasmtime run` / `wasmtime serve`.

GHSA-r8xh-cgf7-392j.title: wasi-http: Guests can add conflicting content lengths to messages
GHSA-r8xh-cgf7-392j.description: ### Summary Guests can make the host send HTTP requests with multiple, conflicting content-length headers. This could be a vector for request-smuggling attacks when handled by servers or intermediaries which do not treat this condition as an error. Now, guests are only allowed to set a single value for the content-length header. ### Patches Patches are present in main and 50.0.0, and patch releases 36.0.19, 48.0.7 and 49.0.4.

GHSA-vcg5-q8m5-8379.title: Wasmtime may not properly enforce async-entrypoint requirement
GHSA-vcg5-q8m5-8379.description: ### Summary A `Store` in Wasmtime has insufficient checks when mixing async-style and sync-style calls into WebAssembly when the store otherwise does not require async calls to be performed. This can lead to arbitrary host code being suspended and moved across threads, which can be unsound with `!Send` local variables for example, or internal panics within the runtime itself due to unexpected scenarios being hit. ## Impact This bug can lead to panics within the runtime in certain scheduling situations. This bug can additionally lead to unsoundness in arbitrary host code if `!Send` variables, such as `Rc<T>`, are present on the stack. Wasmtime typically statically disallows this at compile time, but the missing checks for this issue failed to check this condition. This bug is not controllable from guest-code, however, and requires the host to manually re-enter WebAssembly from host functions via sync-style APIs while originally calling WebAssembly via async-style APIs. This vulnerability requires this specific shape of embedder code to be written or otherwise this is inapplicable. If an embedder doesn't use async at all, then they are unaffected. All preexisting versions of Wasmtime after 42.0.0 are affected by this issue. ## Patches Wasmtime 48.0.6 and 49.0.3 have been released fixing this issue. ## Workarounds If the store otherwise requires async entrypoints to be used, such as an async host function being defined, will correctly require all entrypoints to use async.

GHSA-wjc8-633q-pwxr.title: Stack overflow dropping a long chain of recursive types
GHSA-wjc8-633q-pwxr.description: ### Impact Guests can trigger a crash in the host by defining a long chain of types which causes the host to stack overflow when removing the top level type from the type registry. This was caused because dropping one type can remove all references to an inner type and trigger a recursive call to drop that inner type which generates a stack who's depth is controlled by the length of the type chain. The dropping logic was originally protected against this guest-controlled recursion by converting it into an iterative loop, but recursion was accidentally introduced in Wasmtime 42.0.0. So all versions >= 42.0.0 are affected. ### Patches The fix is present in main and patch releases are made for 48.0.6 and 49.0.3. ### Workarounds There are no known workarounds.

GHSA-5qpp-g3j2-8frx.description: ### Summary Wasmtime's implementation of `wasi:http` in the `wasmtime-wasi-http` crate did not check that the value a guest passes to `set-path-with-query` on an outgoing request is actually a path. However, RFC 9112 requires a server receiving an absolute-form target to ignore `Host`, so if the allowed authority is a forward proxy or a gateway that honors absolute-form targets, it forwards the request to `other.example`. A guest may then reach hosts the embedder did not have visibility into or allow. Both `wasi:http@0.2` and `wasi:http@0.3` are affected, including guests run with `wasmtime serve` and `wasmtime run -S http`. ### Impact This issue can cause hosts using the `wasmtime-wasi-http` crate to erroneously have requests sent to hosts that are otherwise explicitly disallowed in filtering policies. ### Patches Wasmtime 36.0.18, 48.0.6, and 49.0.3 have all been released which fixes this issue.

GHSA-6fr9-xmw9-5352.title: Unchecked memory usage in transferring borrowed resources between components
GHSA-6fr9-xmw9-5352.description: ### Summary Wasmtime contained a denial-of-service vulnerability where host memory could arbitrarily be consumed by transferring borrowed resources between components. This is similar to a previous vulnerability GHSA-q554-3cjc-rx7p but affects a different path which was not fixed there. Specifically when a component receives a borrowed resource that it defined itself there is no handle counter incremented charged to the store, but Wasmtime still allocated host memory to track this borrow. This memory allocation wasn't accounted for anywhere and guests could make this memory grow arbitrarily large. ### Details Wasmtime's tracking of `borrow<T>` handles in the component model employs host-allocated resources to be able to handle what happens when a function returns and undo the 'lends' of the `own<T>` resource they originally came from, as required by component model semantics. This tracking is handled specially, according to the component model, when a component receives a borrow for a resource it itself defines. In this situation the component does not receive a handle but instead receives its internal representation. This difference means that the mitigation implemented in GHSA-q554-3cjc-rx7p is bypassed as there's no handle that's charged to the store which is limited by default. Combined together it means that a lent borrow is untracked memory not limited by any means. ### Impact This is a denial-of-service vulnerability for Wasmtime where a guest can consume arbitrary host memory. Hosts are affected in default configurations and there is no known mitigation for this. Affected hosts are recommended to update to a patched version.

GHSA-h4wp-g4x3-7398.title: wasi-http p2: outgoing content-length can be invalid or not match body
GHSA-h4wp-g4x3-7398.description: ### Summary The wasmtime-wasi-http p2 implementation can, in some cases, send multiple conflicting content-length headers, or a content-length header which does not match the body length. This can expose other HTTP implementations to request smuggling attacks, bypassing the access control mechanisms built into wasmtime-wasi-http. ### Details This bug is related to GHSA-r8xh-cgf7-392j, which fixed wasmtime-wasi-http's handling of invalid content-length headers. The remediation of that bug unintentionally left one gap in enforcement. When a wasip2 guest receives a content-length header (or multiple, conflicting content-length headers) in an HTTP response, and then uses that headers resource to construct a HTTP request, and that request is sent without setting a body, the request will contain the response's content-length headers, and those could be conflicting and (unless it is the benign `content-length: 0`) will not match the body length. This particular pattern of use was, we believe, the only corner case not covered by previous remediation and testing. ### Impact This could enable HTTP request/response smuggling attacks (CWE-444) when used to send a request to a server which does not correctly implement HTTP. This attach mechanism could potentially bypass the access control mechanisms used by wasmtime-wasi-http embedders to restrict the destination of an HTTP request.

GHSA-m9f7-9w4p-gv38.title: Filesystem sandbox escape when renaming symlinks with trailing slashes
GHSA-m9f7-9w4p-gv38.description: ## Impact Wasmtime's filesystem implementation provided in the `wasmtime-wasi` crate contained a bug which allowed guests to escape their filesystem sandbox and read/write external directories. Guests provided write-access to any directory within their sandbox could move any directory on the filesystem the host process could access into their sandbox, and then read and write its contents. This bug is a full filesystem sandbox escape for guests. This bug is closely related to [GHSA-vqjp-4c8c-hfgg](https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/security/advisories/GHSA-vqjp-4c8c-hfgg). When renaming a file or directory, `wasmtime-wasi` strips a trailing slash from the source path to resolve its parent directory, but then re-appends the slash to the final path component before passing it to the `renameat` syscall. A guest could create a relative symlink pointing outside of its sandbox, for example `symlink('../outside', 'up')`, and then rename `'up/'` to a path within its sandbox. The host kernel would then follow the trailing-slash symlink and move the directory outside of the sandbox into the sandbox. The fix for GHSA-vqjp-4c8c-hfgg only changed how paths are opened, not how they are renamed, so this affects all published versions of Wasmtime at the time of this advisory's publication. This bug does not affect users on Linux or Windows, where `renameat` does not follow a symlink with a trailing slash. Users on macOS or FreeBSD, however, are affected by this issue. Only symlinks to directories can be used to escape the sandbox in this manner. ## Patches Wasmtime 36.0.18, 48.0.6, and 49.0.3 are being released with this advisory which patches this issue. ## Workarounds There is no known workaround for this issue. Users are recommended to upgrade to a patch release of Wasmtime that contains a fixed version of `wasmtime-wasi`. ## References * [GHSA-vqjp-4c8c-hfgg](https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/security/advisories/GHSA-vqjp-4c8c-hfgg) * bytecodealliance/wasmtime#14663 (the related `remove_dir` case)

GHSA-q554-3cjc-rx7p.title: Component-model handle tables are capped only per instance and charged to no limit
GHSA-q554-3cjc-rx7p.description: ### Summary A malicious guest can drive unbounded host memory growth using only component-model resource handles, with no linear memory, no core tables, no host imports, and default configuration. ### Impact Each guest `resource.new` allocates a slot in the owning component instance's host-side handle table. Allocation is bounded only by a per-table cap and is charged to no `ResourceLimiter` or `StoreLimits`, so `-W max-memory-size` and the embedder's configured memory and table limits do not bound it. Because the cap is per component instance, a single component can exceed it many times over by instantiating a sub-component repeatedly. ## Patches Wasmtime 49.0.3, 48.0.6, and 36.0.18 have been fixed by introducing a store-wide limit on the number of simultaneously-live component-model handles. - Default limit: **100,000 live handles per store** (~2.4 MB of handle-table memory). - New embedder knob: `Store::set_max_component_handles(n)` to raise or lower it. - New CLI flag: `-S max-component-handles=N` for `wasmtime run` / `wasmtime serve`.

GHSA-r8xh-cgf7-392j.description: ### Summary Guests can make the host send HTTP requests with multiple, conflicting content-length headers. This could be a vector for request-smuggling attacks when handled by servers or intermediaries which do not treat this condition as an error. Now, guests are only allowed to set a single value for the content-length header. ### Patches Patches are present in main and 50.0.0, and patch releases 36.0.19, 48.0.7 and 49.0.4.

GHSA-vcg5-q8m5-8379.title: Wasmtime may not properly enforce async-entrypoint requirement
GHSA-vcg5-q8m5-8379.description: ### Summary A `Store` in Wasmtime has insufficient checks when mixing async-style and sync-style calls into WebAssembly when the store otherwise does not require async calls to be performed. This can lead to arbitrary host code being suspended and moved across threads, which can be unsound with `!Send` local variables for example, or internal panics within the runtime itself due to unexpected scenarios being hit. ## Impact This bug can lead to panics within the runtime in certain scheduling situations. This bug can additionally lead to unsoundness in arbitrary host code if `!Send` variables, such as `Rc<T>`, are present on the stack. Wasmtime typically statically disallows this at compile time, but the missing checks for this issue failed to check this condition. This bug is not controllable from guest-code, however, and requires the host to manually re-enter WebAssembly from host functions via sync-style APIs while originally calling WebAssembly via async-style APIs. This vulnerability requires this specific shape of embedder code to be written or otherwise this is inapplicable. If an embedder doesn't use async at all, then they are unaffected. All preexisting versions of Wasmtime after 42.0.0 are affected by this issue. ## Patches Wasmtime 48.0.6 and 49.0.3 have been released fixing this issue. ## Workarounds If the store otherwise requires async entrypoints to be used, such as an async host function being defined, will correctly require all entrypoints to use async.

GHSA-wjc8-633q-pwxr.title: Stack overflow dropping a long chain of recursive types
GHSA-wjc8-633q-pwxr.description: ### Impact Guests can trigger a crash in the host by defining a long chain of types which causes the host to stack overflow when removing the top level type from the type registry. This was caused because dropping one type can remove all references to an inner type and trigger a recursive call to drop that inner type which generates a stack who's depth is controlled by the length of the type chain. The dropping logic was originally protected against this guest-controlled recursion by converting it into an iterative loop, but recursion was accidentally introduced in Wasmtime 42.0.0. So all versions >= 42.0.0 are affected. ### Patches The fix is present in main and patch releases are made for 48.0.6 and 49.0.3. ### Workarounds There are no known workarounds.

Absolute-form values such as `http://other.example/x` were accepted and written verbatim as the request target of the HTTP/1.1 request line, while the connection and the `Host` header used the authority the guest set with `set-authority`: ``` GET http://other.example/x HTTP/1.1 host: allowed.example ``` Wasmtime only connects to the authority the guest set, and any sort of request filtering based on host is done by the authority the guest set as well. However, RFC 9112 requires a server receiving an absolute-form target to ignore `Host`, so if the allowed authority is a forward proxy or a gateway that honors absolute-form targets, it forwards the request to `other.example`. A guest may then reach hosts the embedder did not have visibility into or allow. Both `wasi:http@0.2` and `wasi:http@0.3` are affected, including guests run with `wasmtime serve` and `wasmtime run -S http`. ### Impact This issue can cause hosts using the `wasmtime-wasi-http` crate to erroneously have requests sent to hosts that are otherwise explicitly disallowed in filtering policies. ### Patches Wasmtime 36.0.18, 48.0.6, and 49.0.3 have all been released which fixes this issue.

GHSA-6fr9-xmw9-5352.title: Unchecked memory usage in transferring borrowed resources between components
GHSA-6fr9-xmw9-5352.description: ### Summary Wasmtime contained a denial-of-service vulnerability where host memory could arbitrarily be consumed by transferring borrowed resources between components. This is similar to a previous vulnerability GHSA-q554-3cjc-rx7p but affects a different path which was not fixed there. Specifically when a component receives a borrowed resource that it defined itself there is no handle counter incremented charged to the store, but Wasmtime still allocated host memory to track this borrow. This memory allocation wasn't accounted for anywhere and guests could make this memory grow arbitrarily large. ### Details Wasmtime's tracking of `borrow<T>` handles in the component model employs host-allocated resources to be able to handle what happens when a function returns and undo the 'lends' of the `own<T>` resource they originally came from, as required by component model semantics. This tracking is handled specially, according to the component model, when a component receives a borrow for a resource it itself defines. In this situation the component does not receive a handle but instead receives its internal representation. This difference means that the mitigation implemented in GHSA-q554-3cjc-rx7p is bypassed as there's no handle that's charged to the store which is limited by default. Combined together it means that a lent borrow is untracked memory not limited by any means. ### Impact This is a denial-of-service vulnerability for Wasmtime where a guest can consume arbitrary host memory. Hosts are affected in default configurations and there is no known mitigation for this. Affected hosts are recommended to update to a patched version.

GHSA-h4wp-g4x3-7398.title: wasi-http p2: outgoing content-length can be invalid or not match body
GHSA-h4wp-g4x3-7398.description: ### Summary The wasmtime-wasi-http p2 implementation can, in some cases, send multiple conflicting content-length headers, or a content-length header which does not match the body length. This can expose other HTTP implementations to request smuggling attacks, bypassing the access control mechanisms built into wasmtime-wasi-http. ### Details This bug is related to GHSA-r8xh-cgf7-392j, which fixed wasmtime-wasi-http's handling of invalid content-length headers. The remediation of that bug unintentionally left one gap in enforcement. When a wasip2 guest receives a content-length header (or multiple, conflicting content-length headers) in an HTTP response, and then uses that headers resource to construct a HTTP request, and that request is sent without setting a body, the request will contain the response's content-length headers, and those could be conflicting and (unless it is the benign `content-length: 0`) will not match the body length. This particular pattern of use was, we believe, the only corner case not covered by previous remediation and testing. ### Impact This could enable HTTP request/response smuggling attacks (CWE-444) when used to send a request to a server which does not correctly implement HTTP. This attach mechanism could potentially bypass the access control mechanisms used by wasmtime-wasi-http embedders to restrict the destination of an HTTP request.

GHSA-m9f7-9w4p-gv38.title: Filesystem sandbox escape when renaming symlinks with trailing slashes
GHSA-m9f7-9w4p-gv38.description: ## Impact Wasmtime's filesystem implementation provided in the `wasmtime-wasi` crate contained a bug which allowed guests to escape their filesystem sandbox and read/write external directories. Guests provided write-access to any directory within their sandbox could move any directory on the filesystem the host process could access into their sandbox, and then read and write its contents. This bug is a full filesystem sandbox escape for guests. This bug is closely related to [GHSA-vqjp-4c8c-hfgg](https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/security/advisories/GHSA-vqjp-4c8c-hfgg). When renaming a file or directory, `wasmtime-wasi` strips a trailing slash from the source path to resolve its parent directory, but then re-appends the slash to the final path component before passing it to the `renameat` syscall. A guest could create a relative symlink pointing outside of its sandbox, for example `symlink('../outside', 'up')`, and then rename `'up/'` to a path within its sandbox. The host kernel would then follow the trailing-slash symlink and move the directory outside of the sandbox into the sandbox. The fix for GHSA-vqjp-4c8c-hfgg only changed how paths are opened, not how they are renamed, so this affects all published versions of Wasmtime at the time of this advisory's publication. This bug does not affect users on Linux or Windows, where `renameat` does not follow a symlink with a trailing slash. Users on macOS or FreeBSD, however, are affected by this issue. Only symlinks to directories can be used to escape the sandbox in this manner. ## Patches Wasmtime 36.0.18, 48.0.6, and 49.0.3 are being released with this advisory which patches this issue. ## Workarounds There is no known workaround for this issue. Users are recommended to upgrade to a patch release of Wasmtime that contains a fixed version of `wasmtime-wasi`. ## References * [GHSA-vqjp-4c8c-hfgg](https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/security/advisories/GHSA-vqjp-4c8c-hfgg) * bytecodealliance/wasmtime#14663 (the related `remove_dir` case)

GHSA-q554-3cjc-rx7p.title: Component-model handle tables are capped only per instance and charged to no limit
GHSA-q554-3cjc-rx7p.description: ### Summary A malicious guest can drive unbounded host memory growth using only component-model resource handles, with no linear memory, no core tables, no host imports, and default configuration. ### Impact Each guest `resource.new` allocates a slot in the owning component instance's host-side handle table. Allocation is bounded only by a per-table cap and is charged to no `ResourceLimiter` or `StoreLimits`, so `-W max-memory-size` and the embedder's configured memory and table limits do not bound it. Because the cap is per component instance, a single component can exceed it many times over by instantiating a sub-component repeatedly. ## Patches Wasmtime 49.0.3, 48.0.6, and 36.0.18 have been fixed by introducing a store-wide limit on the number of simultaneously-live component-model handles. - Default limit: **100,000 live handles per store** (~2.4 MB of handle-table memory). - New embedder knob: `Store::set_max_component_handles(n)` to raise or lower it. - New CLI flag: `-S max-component-handles=N` for `wasmtime run` / `wasmtime serve`.

GHSA-r8xh-cgf7-392j.title: wasi-http: Guests can add conflicting content lengths to messages
GHSA-r8xh-cgf7-392j.description: ### Summary Guests can make the host send HTTP requests with multiple, conflicting content-length headers. This could be a vector for request-smuggling attacks when handled by servers or intermediaries which do not treat this condition as an error. Now, guests are only allowed to set a single value for the content-length header. ### Patches Patches are present in main and 50.0.0, and patch releases 36.0.19, 48.0.7 and 49.0.4.

GHSA-vcg5-q8m5-8379.title: Wasmtime may not properly enforce async-entrypoint requirement
GHSA-vcg5-q8m5-8379.description: ### Summary A `Store` in Wasmtime has insufficient checks when mixing async-style and sync-style calls into WebAssembly when the store otherwise does not require async calls to be performed. This can lead to arbitrary host code being suspended and moved across threads, which can be unsound with `!Send` local variables for example, or internal panics within the runtime itself due to unexpected scenarios being hit. ## Impact This bug can lead to panics within the runtime in certain scheduling situations. This bug can additionally lead to unsoundness in arbitrary host code if `!Send` variables, such as `Rc<T>`, are present on the stack. Wasmtime typically statically disallows this at compile time, but the missing checks for this issue failed to check this condition. This bug is not controllable from guest-code, however, and requires the host to manually re-enter WebAssembly from host functions via sync-style APIs while originally calling WebAssembly via async-style APIs. This vulnerability requires this specific shape of embedder code to be written or otherwise this is inapplicable. If an embedder doesn't use async at all, then they are unaffected. All preexisting versions of Wasmtime after 42.0.0 are affected by this issue. ## Patches Wasmtime 48.0.6 and 49.0.3 have been released fixing this issue. ## Workarounds If the store otherwise requires async entrypoints to be used, such as an async host function being defined, will correctly require all entrypoints to use async.

GHSA-wjc8-633q-pwxr.title: Stack overflow dropping a long chain of recursive types
GHSA-wjc8-633q-pwxr.description: ### Impact Guests can trigger a crash in the host by defining a long chain of types which causes the host to stack overflow when removing the top level type from the type registry. This was caused because dropping one type can remove all references to an inner type and trigger a recursive call to drop that inner type which generates a stack who's depth is controlled by the length of the type chain. The dropping logic was originally protected against this guest-controlled recursion by converting it into an iterative loop, but recursion was accidentally introduced in Wasmtime 42.0.0. So all versions >= 42.0.0 are affected. ### Patches The fix is present in main and patch releases are made for 48.0.6 and 49.0.3. ### Workarounds There are no known workarounds.

CVE-2026-115387.title: Wasmtime before 36.0.16, 37.0.0 before 48.0.3, and 49.0.0 before  ...

CVE-2026-115389.title: Wasmtime before 36.0.16, 37.0.0 before 48.0.3, and 49.0.0 before  ...

CVE-2026-115392.title: Wasmtime before 24.0.13, 25.0.0 before 36.0.14, 37.0.0 before 46. ...
CVE-2026-115392.description: Wasmtime before 24.0.13, 25.0.0 before 36.0.14, 37.0.0 before 46.0.3, and 47.0.0 before 47.0.4 allows a filesystem sandbox escape in wasmtime-wasi because its cap-std dependency mishandles symlinks with trailing slashes on macOS and Linux kernels lacking openat2. CVE-2026-115393.title: Wasmtime before 24.0.12, 25.0.0 before 36.0.13, 37.0.0 before 46. ...
CVE-2026-115393.description: Wasmtime before 24.0.12, 25.0.0 before 36.0.13, 37.0.0 before 46.0.2, and 47.0.0 before 47.0.3 contains a type confusion vulnerability because several Store APIs fail to validate that objects belong to the Store's Engine. CVE-2026-115893.title: Wasmtime is a runtime for WebAssembly. Prior to 36.0.19, 48.0.7,  ...
CVE-2026-115893.description: Wasmtime is a runtime for WebAssembly. This issue is fixed in versions 36.0.19, 48.0.7, and 49.0.4.

CVE-2026-118688.title: wasmtime-wasi in Wasmtime before 36.0.18, 37.0.0 before 48.0.6, a ...

CVE-2026-119134.title: Wasmtime before 36.0.18, 37.0.0 before 48.0.6, and 49.0.0 before  ...

CVE-2026-119137.title: Wasmtime 42.0.0 before 48.0.6 and 49.0.0 before 49.0.3 contains a ...
CVE-2026-119137.description: Wasmtime 42.0.0 before 48.0.6 and 49.0.0 before 49.0.3 contains a stack overflow vulnerability that allows guests to crash the host through recursive type drops. CVE-2026-121441.title: Wasmtime before 36.0.19, 37.0.0 before 48.0.7, and 49.0.0 before  ...
CVE-2026-121441.description: Wasmtime before 36.0.19, 37.0.0 before 48.0.7, and 49.0.0 before 49.0.4 contains a request smuggling vulnerability in wasi-http that allows guests to set multiple conflicting content-length headers. CVE-2026-47261.title: Wasmtime is a runtime for WebAssembly. In versions prior to 24.0. ...
CVE-2026-47261.description: Wasmtime is a runtime for WebAssembly. In versions prior to 24.0.9, 36.0.10, and 44.0.2, when a filesystem preopen is given DirPerms::all() and FilePerms::READ without FilePerms::WRITE, this access control mechanism can be bypassed via the wasip2 descriptor.open-at or wasip1 path_open interfaces by opening a file with only the OpenFlags::TRUNCATE oflag. The root cause is that the clause handling OpenFlags::TRUNCATE in crates/wasi/src/filesystem.rs (Dir::open_at, lines 967–969) did not set open_mode |= OpenMode::WRITE;, which is later used for the access control check against FilePerms to determine whether opening the file is permitted; the single-line fix adds that missing assignment, after which the affected calls correctly fail with error-code.not-permitted and ERRNO_PERM respectively. Only wasmtime-wasi embeddings that combine DirPerms::MUTATE with FilePerms::READ are affected by this bug. In particular, the Wasmtime project's wasmtime-cli's use of wasmtime-wasi is not affected, because it always sets FilePerms::all() for all preopens. This issue has been fixed in versions 24.0.9, 36.0.10 and44.0.2.

CVE-2026-54786.title: Wasmtime is a runtime for WebAssembly. All versions prior to 24.0 ...
CVE-2026-54786.description: Wasmtime is a runtime for WebAssembly. All versions prior to 24.0.10; versions 25.0.0 through those before  36.0.11; versions 37.0.0 through those before 44.0.3; and versions 45.0.0 and 45.0.1 contain a native implementation of WASIp1 which suffers from a leak in the fd_renumber function where the file descriptor being renumbered to is not properly closed. Wasmtime's implementation erroneously only updated the table of descriptors for WASIp1 and didn't update the underlying table of descriptors used by the host. This behavior means that while fd_renumber works correctly from a guest's perspective it ends up leaking resources in the host that aren't cleaned up until the corresponding Store is destroyed. In a loop, guests can use fd_renumber to cause hosts to exhaust both resources and file descriptors. This bug only affects the native implementation of WASIp1, meaning that only runtimes which load core wasm modules and expose fd_renumber are affected. Runtimes are additionally only affected if they expose the ability to acquire a file descriptor, such as opening a file. For runtimes that deny access to files they are unaffected. This issue has been fixed in versions 24.0.10, 36.0.11, 44.0.3, and 45.0.2.

CVE-2026-58494.title: Wasmtime is a runtime for WebAssembly. Prior to 24.0.11, 36.0.12, ...
CVE-2026-58494.description: Wasmtime is a runtime for WebAssembly. Prior to 24.0.11, 36.0.12, 45.0.3, and 46.0.1, wasmtime-wasi hard-link creation and renaming check directory permissions but not matching FilePerms on source and destination preopens, allowing a WASI guest with a read-only source file capability to overwrite host files exposed as FilePerms::READ through wasip1, wasip2, or wasip3 filesystem interfaces. This issue is fixed in versions 24.0.11, 36.0.12, 45.0.3, and 46.0.1.

GHSA-6fr9-xmw9-5352.title: Unchecked memory usage in transferring borrowed resources between components
GHSA-6fr9-xmw9-5352.description: ### Summary Wasmtime contained a denial-of-service vulnerability where host memory could arbitrarily be consumed by transferring borrowed resources between components. Specifically when a component receives a borrowed resource that it defined itself there is no handle counter incremented charged to the store, but Wasmtime still allocated host memory to track this borrow. This memory allocation wasn't accounted for anywhere and guests could make this memory grow arbitrarily large. ### Details Wasmtime's tracking of `borrow<T>` handles in the component model employs host-allocated resources to be able to handle what happens when a function returns and undo the 'lends' of the `own<T>` resource they originally came from, as required by component model semantics. This tracking is handled specially, according to the component model, when a component receives a borrow for a resource it itself defines. In this situation the component does not receive a handle but instead receives its internal representation. This difference means that the mitigation implemented in GHSA-q554-3cjc-rx7p is bypassed as there's no handle that's charged to the store which is limited by default. Combined together it means that a lent borrow is untracked memory not limited by any means. ### Impact This is a denial-of-service vulnerability for Wasmtime where a guest can consume arbitrary host memory. Hosts are affected in default configurations and there is no known mitigation for this. Affected hosts are recommended to update to a patched version.

GHSA-h4wp-g4x3-7398.title: wasi-http p2: outgoing content-length can be invalid or not match body
GHSA-h4wp-g4x3-7398.description: ### Summary The wasmtime-wasi-http p2 implementation can, in some cases, send multiple conflicting content-length headers, or a content-length header which does not match the body length. This can expose other HTTP implementations to request smuggling attacks, bypassing the access control mechanisms built into wasmtime-wasi-http. ### Details This bug is related to GHSA-r8xh-cgf7-392j, which fixed wasmtime-wasi-http's handling of invalid content-length headers. The remediation of that bug unintentionally left one gap in enforcement. When a wasip2 guest receives a content-length header (or multiple, conflicting content-length headers) in an HTTP response, and then uses that headers resource to construct a HTTP request, and that request is sent without setting a body, the request will contain the response's content-length headers, and those could be conflicting and (unless it is the benign `content-length: 0`) will not match the body length. This particular pattern of use was, we believe, the only corner case not covered by previous remediation and testing. ### Impact This could enable HTTP request/response smuggling attacks (CWE-444) when used to send a request to a server which does not correctly implement HTTP. This attach mechanism could potentially bypass the access control mechanisms used by wasmtime-wasi-http embedders to restrict the destination of an HTTP request.

GHSA-m9f7-9w4p-gv38.description: ## Impact Wasmtime's filesystem implementation provided in the `wasmtime-wasi` crate contained a bug which allowed guests to escape their filesystem sandbox and read/write external directories.
